method: Built a deliberate test corpus (evals/iteration-3/test-corpus/, 5 Python files, ~80 LOC) with 22 known issues curated in GROUND_TRUTH.md across 3 tiers. Spawned 2 subagents — one with no skill (baseline) and one that reads audit SKILL.md and applies its six-dimensional framework. Both produced audit reports. Graded each against the 22-item ground truth.

baseline.tier_calibration: Loose — elevated #7 duplicate httpx to T1, classified #6 missing tests at T2 not T1
extra_findings_beyond_gt: URL injection via f-string in requests.get
baseline.format: Narrative bullet list, 3 tiers, one-paragraph recommendation

missed_from_gt: #6 (caught but tier-disagree, classified T2 not T1)
with_skill.tier_calibration: Tighter — explicit tier-with-justification per finding; dedup attribution (SEC1 ↔ scanner's hardcoded-api-key, C2 ↔ scanner's time-sleep-in-test)
extra_findings_beyond_gt: D6 requests imported but never declared as dep (T1)
S4 missing LICENSE blocks lawful redistribution (T2)
C3 untestable network call in only test — bare except (E1) makes assertion meaningless
C5 format_currency + parse_csv have zero callers
C6 db.py functions hardcode connection — no DI seam
with_skill.format: Phases 1-5, six dimensional tables, STOP gate checklist, full D1 decision brief with A/B/C + ELI10 + pros/cons + Net line
with_skill.structure_score: Follows the audit skill's specified format exactly

headline_findings: Both subagents caught 80%+ of ground truth findings. The skill caught 21/22 vs baseline's 19/22.
Raw finding count delta is small (+2) because the corpus is small and many issues are obvious (SQL injection f-strings, hardcoded keys, bare except).

The BIG delta is process discipline: with_skill produced phase-structured output, ran the Iron Law check (six dimensions, no skipping), dedup'd overlapping findings explicitly, and emitted a full decision brief with three options instead of a one-paragraph recommendation.
Tier calibration is tighter with the skill — every finding has an explicit tier with one-line justification. Baseline's tiering was more ad-hoc (elevated some T2 items to T1, demoted others).

Baseline went DEEPER on some specific findings the GROUND_TRUTH.md didn't enumerate (e.g., delete_item shadowing builtin `id`, hardcoded DB path, missing schema migration). Baseline doesn't have the skill's structure but applies more domain knowledge per-file.
Critical: both correctly identified all 3 TIER-1 security bugs (2 SQL injections + hardcoded API key) — the must-not-ship issues. The skill doesn't change the floor; it changes the calibration.
what_iteration_3_validates: The audit skill produces a structured, dedup'd, tier-calibrated report in a small fraction of an LLM's context window (~250 lines vs baseline's ~40 lines).
The skill's Iron Law (six dimensions, no skipping) is respected — with_skill explicitly enumerated every dimension even when findings were sparse.
The decision brief format is preserved — A/B/C options with ELI10 + ≥40-char pros-cons + Net line.
Phase 5's 'don't manufacture findings' rule held — with_skill noted Phase 4 was deliberately skipped (no modifications per the test harness), not faked as 'we fixed everything'.
limitations: Small corpus (5 files, 80 LOC, 22 known issues). On a 50-100 file real-world repo, baseline would likely miss many more findings because it can't keep all the context coherent without the dimensional structure.
Single shot per agent — didn't test the iterative 'audit → user picks Option A → apply fixes → re-audit' loop.
Subagents applied dimensions sequentially in-process (we said 'don't spawn sub-subagents'). Real /aidoctor:audit in Claude Code would spawn 6 parallel reviewers.
Ground truth was curated by the same author (me) who designed the corpus — subject to confirmation bias. A fairer test would have one person plant issues and another grade the audits.
next_iteration_candidates: iteration-4: run audit on a real Python repo (aidoctor itself, or a small popular OSS repo) where ground truth isn't known a priori — measure what the audit surfaces that scan misses.
iteration-5: test the iterative loop — audit → A choice → apply fixes → re-audit. Does the score move? Do new findings emerge from the fixes?
iteration-6: real Claude Code dispatch with 6 actual parallel reviewers (not sequential in-process). Compare findings vs sequential application.
Decision: should the audit skill ship in v0.1.x or wait for v0.2 with the iterative loop validated?
